title: Databrary Guide
text:
Welcome
This document describes the Databrary.org data library and how to use it effectively as a tool for safely and securely sharing identifiable research data including video and audio.
Databrary is used by a large and growing community of researchers across the globe. The widespread use and sharing of video can improve reproducibility and rigor of many different areas of research (Adolph, K.E., Gilmore, R.O., & Kennedy, J.L., 2017; Gilmore & Adolph, 2017).
Databrary’s mission is to support data sharing and reuse among researchers in the behavioral, social, educational, developmental, neural, and computer sciences. The platform is dedicated to advancing transparency, reproducibility, and collaboration across the research community. Databrary serves as a community of scientists and a resource for those who use video or audio in their research or teaching.

Our Team
Based at New York University, Databrary is the world’s only large-scale data repository specializing in storing and sharing research videos in behavioral sciences and the broader research community. It supports the storing, streaming, and sharing of video and audio recordings along with a wide range of research materials such as transcriptions, images, and metadata.

title: Why Databrary?
text:
Our Framework
Data repositories and libraries provide permanent homes for research findings and raw data. Sharing research data is a vital component of the research process, just like publishing papers and books, giving talks, and teaching classes. Open science and sharing information is how we advance as a community.
Many granting agencies require that research data be shared. As an NIH-approved repository, Databrary provides NIH grantees with a compliant and streamlined way to fulfill their data-sharing obligations.
Videos are expensive and time consuming to collect and annotate. Sharing and reusing videos accelerates discovery. Researchers across fields can reuse video data and glean insights beyond those of the original data contributor.
Databrary is structured on a framework of open sharing with restricted access. Open sharing on Databrary allows researchers to reuse data without contacting the original data contributor. However, access to Databrary is restricted to authorized investigators who have completed the formal agreement between the researcher’s institution and New York University, the host institution for Databrary. The formal agreement states that the researcher is affiliated with their institution and that the institution will be responsible for the researcher’s relationship with Databrary.
This framework aims to advance the widespread sharing of research data while respecting the privacy of research participants.
We encourage you to read Databrary’s Access Agreement. The agreement provides information about how Databrary is structured and how it should be used. You should get guidance from your institution’s research ethics board (IRB) for reusing data for research purposes.

title: Glossary
text:
Access: Determines which people can view, show, or otherwise use data on Databrary.
Access Role on Volume: When viewing a volume, this label defines the relationship of the individual to the volume owner. The roles are:

“Owner” is the volume owner.
“Owner’s Sponsored Researcher” is a supervised researcher of the volume owner.
“Collaborator” is either an authorized researcher or supervised researcher of an authorized researcher who is not the volume owner.

Approval Source: Authorizing institution or supervising investigator
Approval Source Column: When the volume owner or volume manager is viewing the ‘Manage Access’ page for a volume, in the ‘Collaborator’ table, this column displays the name of the supervising authorized investigator for this individual if the person is a supervised researcher. “Authorized Researcher” is displayed if the individual is an authorized researcher.
Authorized Institution: An academic, research, government, or health entity with an active, signed contract with Databrary.
Authorized Researcher: A researcher who is granted access to Databrary by their institution (including the option to create volumes, own volumes, share volumes, manage collaborators on volumes, supervise researchers, and access restricted-access files shared on Databrary). Authorized researchers must have the equivalent of PI status at their authorizing institution.
Authorized-User Files: Restricted-access files that cannot be redistributed or shown publicly in any form. These are intended for research use only. If files include identifiable participant data, participant(s) must have given permission for access by authorized users.
Authorized Users: Users who can access restricted-access files on shared volumes (i.e., authorized researchers and their supervised researchers with access to restricted-access files) or private files on their own volumes.
Authorizing Institution: An authorized institution that takes responsibility for and can authorize an authorized researcher.
Collaborator on a Volume: An approved user who was explicitly added to the volume by the volume owner but is not supervised by the volume owner. All collaborators must be authorized researchers or supervised researchers who are supervised by an authorized researcher other than the volume owner. Collaborators cannot be people who have yet to be authorized or supervised. Collaborators may be at the owner’s institution or a different institution.
Files: Data inside a volume.
Institutional Admin: A person who manages the authorized institution’s volumes and can grant or revoke access to authorized researchers or other institutional admins.
Institutional Affiliation: An institution that an approved user associates themselves with. Affiliation might be different from the authorizing institution.
Learning-Audience Files: Restricted-access files that can be used for educational, informational, and research purposes. These files can be shown publicly, and presentations may be recorded and made available on the internet (e.g., YouTube). If files include identifiable participant data, participant(s) must have given permission for access by learning audiences.
Participant-Level Files: A set of files accompanied by metadata that relate to an individual or a group of individuals at a particular place and/or time, permissioned at a particular release level.
Private-Access Files: Files that are restricted to the volume owner and individuals chosen by the owner (i.e., supervised researchers or collaborators). If files include identifiable participant data, participant(s) did not give permission for access by authorized users or the public.
Public-Access Files: Files hosted on Databrary that are accessible to anyone on the internet. If files include identifiable participant data, participant(s) must have given permission for public access.
Restricted-Access Files: Files labeled as “Authorized Users” or “Learning Audiences” that are only accessible by authorized users.
Shared Volume: A volume whose owner set access to be visible on Databrary to authorized users who are not the owner’s chosen supervised researchers or collaborators. That is, the volume will be viewable on the internet with a URL that resolves to that volume indefinitely. (A DOI is minted at this point.) Sharing a volume is a deliberate decision that can only be done by the volume owner. Files in a shared volume can be labeled as “Public,” “Learning Audiences,” “Authorized Users,” or “Private.”
Supervising Researcher: A researcher (e.g., student, staff member, post-doctoral fellows, or other person who is not an authorized researcher) who is granted access to Databrary by an authorized researcher who agrees to take responsibility for their use of Databrary.
Supervising Investigator: An authorized researcher who chooses and takes responsibility for (i.e., supervises) a supervised researcher.
Superinstitution: An institution that is granted additional privileges (e.g., to authorize institutions and investigators or remove accounts). Databrary is the only superinstitution.
Unshared Volume: A volume whose owner has set access to be visible on Databrary only to approved users who are the owner’s chosen supervised researchers or collaborators. The default state of a volume is unshared. Files in an unshared volume can be labeled as “Public,” “Learning Audiences,” “Authorized Users,” or “Private.” Regardless of label, until the volume is shared, no files will be visible to anyone on Databrary other than the volume owner and the owner’s chosen supervised researchers and collaborators.
Volume: A dataset or set of files accompanied by metadata. A volume can be owned by either an authorized researcher or an authorized institution.
Volume Manager: An approved user selected by the volume owner who has read/write privileges on a volume, edit the volume name and description, and can propose collaborators. The volume manager cannot share the volume or provide access to collaborators or supervised researchers.
Volume Metadata: Information about a volume or files in the volume.
Volume Owner: The authorized researcher who is responsible for setting access level to the volume to chosen supervised researchers and collaborators and for sharing the volume.
Volume-Level Files: Collection of files in a volume that do not apply to a specific session or individual (they could apply to the entire volume or to a particular set of participants). Such files include annotation manuals, analysis scripts, protocols, survey data, processed data, template consent forms, blank questionnaires, and so on. Files can be set to any access level, but access level for identifiable data must be set based on participant permissions.

title: Ethical Framework
text:
Principles
Many of the most interesting unsolved scientific questions concern behavior of people or non-human animals. Many questions about human and animal behavior are informed and enriched through video and audio recordings that are difficult to de-identify without diminishing their value for future research.
As a restricted access data repository specialized for storing and sharing sensitive and identifiable video research data, Databrary developed an ethical policy framework. The framework allows widespread sharing of unaltered research video while respecting the privacy of human participants.

title: Ethical Framework
text:
The authorized researcher’s institution must be a not-for-profit academic, research, health, or government entity.
The authorized researcher’s institution must have a research ethics board (Institutional Review Board, IRB) to use Databrary materials or contribute data to Databrary.
Authorized researchers must have Principal Investigator status at their institution.
Authorized researchers must take care in authorizing other people (supervised researchers and collaborators) and take responsibility for their conduct and use of Databrary data.
All researchers must ask human participants for their permission to share data and respect participants’ wishes about sharing their data.
All researchers must treat Databrary data with the same high standard of care that they treat data collected in their own laboratory.

title: Ethics for Data Contribution
section: Sharing Data Collected Without a Databrary-Specific Release
text:
Sharing Data Collected Without a Databrary-Specific Release
If you already use a video/audio or photo release form and want to find out whether you can share with Databrary, follow the following steps.

Seek Formal Permission From Your IRB
If your release permits you to show recordings in educational or scientific settings, you may apply for formal permission from your IRB to share these recordings with Databrary.






Note



Databrary intends to store data indefinitely. Some IRBs encourage researchers to include promises to destroy data, especially recordings, after some fixed time period in order to limit risk to participants. Data destruction is antithetical to data sharing, and Databrary’s Template Release language seeks explicit permission to share data indefinitely. NIH and NSF do not require data destruction. Researchers who wish to store Data on Databrary should remove data destruction clauses from their informed consent documents for new data and seek IRB guidance about whether archival data can be shared.




Determine Sharing Release Level
You must ensure that your permission release level matches the correct Databrary sharing release levels.











Share Data with Databrary
You may create a new volume yourself or contact Databrary for help in doing so.

title: Ethics for Data Reuse
text:
Primary Data Collection
The information below is intended to help prepare IRB or ethics board materials for researchers who plan to store and share video data in Databrary.
It may be adapted to suit the specific purposes of the researcher and requirements of the institution. Researchers should confirm institution, agency, directorate/, and program-specific application requirements before submission.
Please contact us at contact@databrary.org for further assistance.
Data will be handled by the team of researchers approved on the IRB protocols of all Principal Investigators and Co-Investigators. Data are linked to participants by subject ID. However, video data are potentially identifiable because participants’ faces are visible and their names may be heard. With participant consent, study data will be stored on Databrary, a secure web-based video library housed at NYU, allowing permission-based access to coders from all labs comprising the project team.
At the end of each lab visit, caregivers will be asked whether they are comfortable:
If caregivers agree to video sharing, the videos will be made available to authorized researchers as outlined below. If caregivers do not agree, their videos will be accessible only by researchers on the project protocol and not shared with the larger community.
Parents will also be told that they can share portions of data or ask for particular sessions not to be shared while sharing other sessions.
The policies for sharing videos and other potentially identifiable data on Databrary have been carefully developed and monitored with the advice of the legal counsel, grants and contracts office, and IRBs of both New York University and The Pennsylvania State University.
Currently, more than 780 institutions in the U.S. and around the world have formally approved the Databrary Access Agreement to enable video sharing and reuse.
If you are using Databrary to store and download video data as part of a collaborative data collection, you must ensure your IRB protocol and data management aligns with Databrary’s technical and security guidelines.

title: Ethics for Data Reuse
text:
Secondary Reuse
This project will conduct secondary analyses of participant data obtained from Databrary, an online platform for the storage, sharing, and re-use of video and other research data.
Participants’ consent for study participation and release of data to Databrary were obtained by the original researcher under the oversight of their institutional review board.
Because there is no direct contact with participants as a part of this project, the level of additional risk to participants is low.

title: Ethics for Data Reuse
text:
Policies for Databrary Access
Sensitive or identifiable data shared with Databrary will only be viewable to and downloadable by authorized users who have been granted secure access by Databrary’s administrators. Select data may be made available to the public, but only as determined by the researcher and on the basis of participant permission.
Only researchers with Principal Investigator status from institutions with Institutional Review Boards or similar review entities, and researchers affiliated with Principal Investigators and under their supervision, are authorized for access.
Authorized users are required to sign a user access agreement that specifies that they will: (1) be responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of the data; (2) abide by ethical principles for treatment of human subjects as mandated by their local Institutional Review Boards; (3) agree not use the data for commercial purposes; and (4) treat data in Databrary with the same high standards of care that they would treat data collected in their own laboratories.

title: Ethics for Data Reuse
text:
Policies for Databrary Data Sharing
Only videos and other identifiable data that have been permissioned for sharing by all the depicted individuals in each recording are made available to the community of authorized Databrary users.
In consultation with ethics board officials at New York University and the Pennsylvania State University, Databrary has developed template Sharing Release forms that contributors can add to their IRB protocol. These forms allow researchers to ask participants for permission to share their data.
Federal policies do not require re-consenting of minor participants when they reach the age of majority, if re-consenting is impractical or otherwise increases risks to participants (e.g., by requiring researchers to maintain links between identifiable information and collected data for extended time periods).

Archival and Preservation of Research Data
Data in Databrary will be preserved indefinitely in a secure data storage facility at New York University (NYU); the facility is managed by the university’s Information Technology Services department. Central IT staff handle storage, network, and backup systems. NYU does routine tape backups that are stored off site and performs regular file fixity checks to monitor the integrity of stored assets.
Federal regulations do not require that data be destroyed after a particular time period if they are stored indefinitely in a recognized repository.

title: For Institutions
text:
What is Databrary?
An institution is defined as an academic, not-for-profit, research, government, or health entity whose employees or students conduct scientific research or educational activities. Research and educational institutions play a central role in the Databrary ecosystem.
This section describes some of those roles and responsibilities. It is designed to answer the questions an official with grants and contracts or research ethics compliance responsibilities might ask.
Much of the material is adapted from the Databrary Access Agreement and its three Annexes.
If you are a researcher, research staff or trainee, you may skip this part.
Databrary is a restricted access data library specialized for storing, streaming, and sharing of video and audio recordings. Databrary’s mission is to support the sharing of video and audio recordings and related data collected as part of research in the social, behavioral, educational, and neural sciences.
The responsibility for protecting research data and research participants is shared among authorized researchers and their supervised researchers, institutions, and Databrary.
Databrary has a multi-pronged approach to fostering the sharing of video and related data while upholding ethical research principles. Access is restricted to authorized researchers whose access must be approved by their institution.
Institutions must provide ethics oversight of Authorized Investigators through a research ethics board or Institutional Review Board (IRB) with standards equivalent to that required to secure Federalwide Assurance (FWA) status from the U.S. Government.
Authorized researchers who share data with others must secure permission to share from research participants and record that permission level for each file stored on Databrary.
In turn, authorized researchers who access Databrary and use data shared by other authorized researchers must follow ethical research principles, including respect for the sharing permissions granted by research participants.
Taken together, these features aim to protect the rights of research participants while reducing barriers to sharing data.

title: Specifics
text:
The Databrary Access Agreement
Databrary restricts access to authorized researchers whose institutions sign a formal Databrary Access Agreement.
The Databrary Access Agreement combines provisions for data use and data contribution. Unlike data use agreements that allow specific individuals access to a particular dataset for a discrete research purpose, the Databrary Access Agreement allows any authorized researcher to access all shared volumes on Databrary and use the volumes for many different institutionally-approved purposes.
In addition, the Databrary Access Agreement permits authorized researchers to upload data and to share it with other authorized researchers in accord with the sharing permissions granted by participants and any required institutional approvals.
Databrary believes that combining data use and data contribution in a single agreement reduces barriers to data sharing, meets emerging funder mandates to share research data, and accelerates progress in research.

title: Specifics
section: The Use of Video Extends Beyond Research
text:
The Use of Video Extends Beyond Research
In addition to its many uses in research, video may be used for a variety of pre-research and non-research uses, such as:

Documentation of methodological details
Demonstration of computer-based tasks
Demonstration of video clips for teaching or scientific presentations

Databrary encourages the storage and sharing of video for all of these purposes, in a manner consistent with subject permissions and institutional approvals.

title: Specifics
section: When to Involve a Research Ethics Board or IRB
text:
When to Involve a Research Ethics Board or IRB
Databrary does not require prior research ethics board or IRB approval for an authorized researcher to be granted access to the system or to use Databrary’s shared resources for non-research, educational, or pre-research uses.
However, in signing the Databrary Access Agreement, all authorized researchers agree to secure research ethics approval whenever their use of Databrary requires it under the Institution’s policies. Institutions determine which cases require research ethics board or IRB review and approval.

title: Specifics
text:
What Data are Shared
Databrary stores and shares:

Images, video, and audio recordings that may be identifiable
Data and metadata that are not typically sensitive
De-identified data

Exact birth dates may be stored for use in calculating participant ages, but exact birth dates are only exposed to authorized researchers or supervised researchers given specific access to the data.
Names, addresses, email addresses, financial information, government ID numbers, detailed geographic location information, and other personally identifiable data elements are not stored and shared on Databrary.

title: Specifics
text:
Securing Permission to Share Data
In order to contribute and share identifiable data with Databrary, authorized researchers must secure permission from research participants and any other people (e.g., research staff) who are recorded to store the recordings on Databrary.
Databrary has developed a Sharing Release Template that informs people depicted in recordings of the potential risks associated with sharing video and other data on Databrary.
The Sharing Release Template is one of the resources that Databrary has made available to researchers. The template may be adapted for use at any institution and added to any research ethics or IRB protocol. However, an institution may require other release language in order to provide equivalent protections.
Whether de-identified or pseudonymized data may be shared with Databrary without seeking explicit permission from research participants depends on the authorized researcher’s institution. Some ethics boards or IRBs may allow de-identified or pseudonymized data to be shared without the explicit permission of the research participant.

title: Specifics
section: Uploading Data and Assigning Sharing Permission Levels
text:
Uploading Data and Assigning Sharing Permission Levels
Authorized researchers who upload data to Databrary must assign the level of data sharing granted by research participants to each file uploaded.









The sharing level assigned to each file by default is Private, meaning that no person other than the authorized researcher who uploaded the file and any supervised researchers granted access by the authorized researcher, may view the file.
All newly created volumes are initially made Private, accessible only to an authorized researcher, any supervised researchers the authorized researcher selects, and any other individual authorized researchers granted specific access to the volume.
An authorized researcher may decide to create an overview of a volume when it is created and make the overview publicly available. The overview can serve as the public face of the volume while the data is being collected and analyzed. This can be useful in documenting progress on a research grant to sponsors. The volume overview does not expose data until the authorized researcher chooses to share the volume publicly.

title: Specifics
text:
Sharing Data on Databrary
The authorized researcher decides when to share the volume with other authorized researchers on Databrary. Typically, authorized researchers share the volume when a paper goes to press or a grant period ends.
This makes the data contained in the volume available to other authorized researchers and possibly the public, in accordance with the sharing levels selected by authorized researchers and to the permission granted by participants. For example, individual data files marked Private remain accessible only to people the authorized researcher specifically selects. Similarly, access to volumes labeled Private remains solely under the control of the authorized researcher.

title: Specifics
text:
Databrary and GDPR
Authorized researchers may collect personal data from research participants who have rights under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). GDPR governs the collection of personal data in the European Economic Area (EEA).
Databrary’s servers are currently located in the United States, and data stored on Databrary may be accessed, downloaded, and re-used by authorized researchers and their supervised researchers located outside of the EEA. There are more than 800 Institutions across the globe that have signed the Databrary Access Agreement.
Databrary maintains a list of authorized researchers who have access to shared research data here.
In seeking permission to collect data from research participants governed by GDPR or similar provisions, Authorized Investigators should communicate to research participants information about who may have access to shared data on Databrary and where the data are stored. Institutions and authorized researchers assume responsibility for ensuring that research participants give sharing data permission that satisfies the provisions of GDPR and for abiding by other provisions of GDPR.
Databrary does not typically store information that links a participant’s identity to specific files unless there is a separate agreement between the authorized researcher, the institution, and Databrary to store this type of data. Therefore, if a research participant requests a copy of data stored on Databrary or the modification or deletion of personal data that is stored on Databrary, the authorized researcher or institution is responsible for responding to the request, not Databrary.
Databrary cannot guarantee that data previously shared with other authorized researchers via Databrary can be retrieved from all authorized researchers who accessed a participant’s personal data prior to its modification or removal. Thus, authorized researchers should communicate to research participants that there are limits to a participant’s right to modify or delete personal data that have already been shared on Databrary. The Sharing Release Template contains language for this purpose.
When accessing data shared by other authorized researchers, institutions and their authorized researchers assume responsibility for ensuring that the sharing permission research participants have given in other contexts outside of the EEA meet relevant GDPR provisions.






Note



Please contact us at contact@databrary.org if you are interested in sharing your data and you are worried about meeting GDPR requirements

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
What is Two-Factor Authentication?
In early 2026 Two Factor Authentication (2FA) was implemented as a required security update.
Databrary requires two-factor authentication (2FA) to protect your account and the sensitive research data you access. This guide will help you set up and use an authenticator app.
Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security to your account. In addition to your password, you’ll need to enter a 6-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone or computer each time you log in.

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
Compatible Authenticator Apps
Any TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) compatible authenticator app will work with Databrary. Here are some common options:

Google Authenticator (iOS/Android) — Free and simple to use. Available on the App Store and Google Play.
Microsoft Authenticator (iOS/Android) — Free, with cloud backup support. Available on the App Store and Google Play.
Duo Mobile (iOS/Android) — Popular in educational institutions. If your institution uses Duo, you may already have this installed. Available on the App Store and Google Play.
Authy (iOS/Android/Desktop) — Free, supports multi-device sync and encrypted cloud backups. Available at authy.com.
Apple Passwords (iOS/macOS) — Built into Apple devices. On iOS 18+ and macOS Sequoia+, use the standalone Passwords app. On older versions, access via Settings → Passwords.
Password Managers — Many password managers like 1Password, Bitwarden, and LastPass include TOTP authenticator functionality.

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
Setting Up Two-Factor Authentication

Download an authenticator app — Choose one of the apps listed above and install it on your device.
Scan the QR code — During registration or login, Databrary will display a QR code. Open your authenticator app and use it to scan the code.
Enter the verification code — Your authenticator app will display a 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds. Enter this code to complete setup.
Save your recovery phrase — After setup, you’ll receive a 12-word recovery phrase. Store this in a safe place — you can use it to regain access if you lose your authenticator device.

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
Can’t Scan the QR Code?
If your authenticator app can’t scan the QR code, you can set up manually:

Click “Can’t scan? Set up manually instead” on the setup screen.
In your authenticator app, choose to add an account manually or enter a setup key.
Enter the setup key shown on the Databrary setup screen. Use these settings:


Type: Time-based (TOTP)
Digits: 6
Time step: 30 seconds
Algorithm: SHA-1

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
Logging In with Two-Factor Authentication

Enter your email and password as usual.
Open your authenticator app and find your Databrary account.
Enter the current 6-digit code shown in the app.







Note



Codes change every 30 seconds. If a code doesn’t work, wait for the next one and try again.

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
Lost Access to Your Authenticator?
If you’ve lost access to your authenticator app:

On the login screen, after entering your password, click “Use recovery phrase instead”.
Enter your 12-word recovery phrase.
You’ll be prompted to set up a new authenticator — scan the new QR code with your authenticator app.







Note



If you don’t have your recovery phrase and can’t access your authenticator app, please contact us for assistance.

title: 2FA Guidelines
text:
Troubleshooting

Code not working?
Make sure the time on your phone is accurate. TOTP codes depend on synchronized time so you must enable automatic time setting on your device.


Multiple Databrary entries?
If you see multiple Databrary entries in your authenticator app, use the most recent one. You can delete older entries.


Switching phones?
Before switching to a new phone, either:

Use an authenticator app that supports cloud backup (ie. Microsoft Authenticator or Authy)
Keep your recovery phrase handy to set up on the new device

Authorize New AffiliateSponsorship Requests

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Step 1: Create a Volume
To contribute data to Databrary, you can create a new volume that will hold the collection of data or materials associated with your research project.
Click on ‘Create Volume’ in the right side of your top navigation bar.

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Note



Only authorized researchers with an active Databrary Access Agreement can create a volume.

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Step 2: Volume Overview
The volume overview contains information about the title, description, internal short name and key words.









Please describe the context of data collection and the types of data that will be uploaded (e.g. video, pictures, coding files, survey data, etc.).

Title
The title could be the title of the publication or a good description of the tasks and/or data involved. For better reuse and discoverability, the title should be informative to external researchers.


Description of Dataset
Below is an example format for the description of the dataset:

This dataset focuses on [Provide a description of behavior, location of study, and participant age range]. Dataset includes [Enter description of tasks, videos, questionnaires, materials, etc.].


Videos were [Provide a general description of what the videos were coded for ie., transcribed for mother speech and child vocalizations; coded for mother and child object interaction; child locomotion and emotion].


This volume contains [List the types of files along with approximate numbers for each. Some examples are provided below]:

xx videos (MP4/MOV files)
xx of Datavyu transcription files (OPF files)
xx of Datavyu coding files (OPF files)
Questionnaire data (.xls file)
Several video exemplars of child behaviors (.mp4 files)
Transcription manual (.docx file)
Coding manual (.docx file)
Scripts for processing and exporting data from Datayu (Ruby)
Materials folder containing stimuli, copies of questionnaires used in study, additional participant demographic information, and other materials utilized for the study
Exemplar study intake video of experimenter with participant


You may not have a complete description of your dataset when you first create your volume. It is best practice to fill out as much information as you have and to add more information as your dataset becomes more complete.
The description can also include the abstract of the paper or any associated products.


Internal Short Name
The only people who can see the internal short name are you and your supervised researchers. You can use whatever lab convention makes the most sense to you.


Keywords
Only volume wwners, co-authors, and authorized researchers can enter keywords. It is best practice to use keywords that would have been used in the associated journal article.

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Step 3: Manage Access
Here, you can choose volume sharing options (ie., shared, overview only, or private) and add collaborators (faculty, staff, students) that already have an account on Databrary that is sponsored by an institution or an authorized investigator.










Sharing Level
Private: The volume is private to you and your chosen supervised researchers and volume collaborators.
Volume Overview Only: The volume’s title and description is visible to authorized Databrary users.
Shared: The volume and its contents are visible, accessible and downloadable to authorized Databrary users.






Important



The sharing level controls public Databrary visibility for your volume. Databrary users will not be able to see your volume and its contents unless your volume is shared.








Note



Only the volume owner can share the volume.




Owner
Databrary requires that volumes have a single owner. Volume owners can transfer ownership of their volume to another authorized researcher or to a registered institution or to Databrary.
Transferring ownership typically happens when the data ownership should be under a co-PI or when an Authorized Investigator moves to a new institution.
When you move to a new institution, you’ll need to work with the relevant parties at your institution and your new institution to determine if and how data you collected there may be transferred to your new institution or be retained by your old institution. This determination is independent of Databrary. You will likely also want to locate where local records of the data are stored.






Important



We advise that Databrary not be the sole source of storage for any research data.


Different institutions make different determinations about data transfer, which can depend on the institutions involved, type of data, project status, and source of funding. We have seen cases where data collected and contributed to Databrary become owned by the original institution (i.e., the old institution becomes the volume owner on Databrary) or they are transferred to another institution and you remain the volume owner (with your new institution sponsoring your Databrary access).


Coauthors
Coauthors are people who should get scholarly credit for your volume. Including someone as a coauthor means their name will show up in the volume citation and the DOI once it gets minted.






Note



Co-authorship does not affect who has access to your volume. If you would like to grant access to your volume, you must add them as a colalborator.




Collaborators
Collaborators are your supervised researchers, co-PIs, or external collaborators that have access to your volume and can view, edit, and/or manage your dataset.

Collaborator Access Levels










Read Only: Collaborator can view and download the datasets in the volume but they will not be able to edit anything.
Read/Write: Collaborator can view, download, and edit the datasets in the volume.
Manager: Collaborator can view, download, and edit the datasets in the volume. They can also create new volumes with the supervising authorized researcher as the owner. In addition, managers can manage all collaborators on the volume and add or remove collaborators.




Step 4: Design Spreadsheet
Here, you can choose all the categories and sub-categories you would like to include in your spreadsheet for participant and session metadata. You will need to select the categories and the fields within each category that apply to your study.









Please select all the categories and fields that you know about, even if the information is constant across the entire dataset or true to every participant or session. This makes your dataset more valuable and enhances its potential for reuse.






Note



You can always remove categories from your volume at any point and the metadata will be retained if you choose to reenable them.

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Entering Data
Now, you can add your data to the volume! You must ensure that you have appropriate participant permissions to share data on Databrary. Please navigate to our Obtaining Permissions page to learn more about obtaining the appropriate participant permissions.










Session vs. Folder
Sessions are used for data related to participant sessions. A session usually involves data from an individual participant while they performed a task or tasks in a specific study location at a defined time.
Folders are used for materials related to the study such as surveys, sample consent forms, and stimuli. Some cases that you would use a folder for are:

Exemplar videos
Coding spreadsheets
Coding manual
Coding scripts
Analysis scripts
Processed data
.readme file on how to use the data



Creating a Session or Folder
Sessions and folders need to be added individually. Once the participant ID is entered, the metadata related to the participant ID will be filled in. Then, the rest of the session information will need to be added individually.


Adding Files to a Session or Folder
To add files to a session or folder:

Find the name of the session or folder that you wish to add files to.
Click the ‘Edit’ icon which will open up a session details page.











You may upload files by either dragging and dropping them into the outlined space or by clicking and selecting the files you wish to upload.












Release Levels
When you have obtained your participant permission, you must determine which Databrary sharing release level should be used for your participant’s data.









The release levels will dictate the level of access to your data once your volume is shared.

Session Release Level
The session release level automatically sets the same release level for all files uploaded under that session from that point forward.









When you first create a session, the release level is automatically set to private. If you would like to change the release level, you must edit it manually.






Note



Changing the session release level does not automatically change the release level to existing files under the session. You must update the file release levels manually if you would like it to match the new session release level.




File Release Level
The file release level is set for a particular file or data asset uploaded under that session that is more or less restrictive than the session release level.






Note



If there are files with less restrictive release levels in your session, your session release level column will display an alert.

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Sharing the Volume
When the volume is ready ie., when a paper goes to press or a grant period ends, the volume owner can share the volume with all authorized Databrary users. This is controlled in the ‘Manage Access’ tab.
Sharing the volume makes the data contained in the dataset available to authorized Databrary users, but only in accordance with the session, folder, and file release levels selected by the volume owner and volume collaborators. Individual data files marked Private remain accessible only to people the volume owner specifically selects.
Once your volume is shared, Databrary will automatically mint a DOI for your volume. This DOI is distinct from any published journal article and can be used to directly index your Databrary volume.
The DOI will replace the Databrary volume URL in the “How to Cite” section.

title: Setting Up a Volume
text:
Example Volumes
These are volumes that you can refer to for guidance about creating a robust Databrary volume:

Practice and proficiency: Factors that facilitate infant walking skill
The impact factor in infant development: Falling like a baby
Infant exuberant object play at home: Immense amounts of time-distributed, variable practice

title: Using Data
text:
Research Purposes
The materials and data on Databrary are intended to accelerate discovery. The Databrary Access Agreement and Annexes and the Terms and Conditions of Use provide formal guidance about policies related to contributing and using data.
The data on Databrary can be used for research purposes and non-research purposes.
Databrary is structured on a framework of open sharing with restricted access. Open sharing on Databrary allows researchers to reuse data without contacting the original data contributor. However, access to Databrary is restricted to authorized investigators who have completed the formal agreement between the researcher’s institution and New York University, the host institution for Databrary. The formal agreement states that the researcher is affiliated with their institution and that the institution will be responsible for the researcher’s relationship with Databrary.
Research uses almost always require ethics board or IRB approval. Please consult your institution’s ethics board or IRB to determine whether your intended use is or is not considered research and proceed accordingly.
For guidance, here is what the NIH constitutes as research.

Downloading data from Databrary is a two-step process.

Download as ZIP
When a file is compressed by Databrary, the name of the file with be prepared with the pathway to find the file. If the file is intended to be used for further analysis, it is important to rename the file to a more descriptive name. The adapted name may interrupt data mining such as the file name “session1” may be renamed to “001-session1”. If you are downloading big sessions, folders, and/or files, downloading is not immediate and it will take a while for Databrary to prepare the data for download. If you are encountering downloading issues, you can try to download the data in smaller chunks.

It is also important to think about your available local storage space when downloading big sessions and/or files.

title: Custom Collections
text:
Why Should I Use Custom Collections?
A custom collection, is a volume that unifies sessions, folders, and files from one or more other volumes and presents it all in one place. The original data stays in the original volume; the custom collection just copies and links to it.
Any volume on Databrary can become a custom collection. As soon as a volume contains at least one link to data in another volume, it is treated and displayed as a custom collection. In a custom collection, you can view the linked volumes, the number of uploaded and linked files, and link data to your other volumes.
Custom collections are an easy way to create a new volume and citable product associated with a publication. For instance, if you have a volume with video data and transcripts, you can use a custom collection to upload annotations associated with a new research product and link those annotations to the original videos and transcripts.

title: Custom Collections
text:
Custom Collection Key Terms

Link Types

Linked volume: An entire volume is linked into the custom collection. All of its sessions and folders appear in the destination.
Linked session: A single session from another volume is linked into the custom collection.
Linked folder: A single folder from another volume is linked into the custom collection.
Linked file: A single file from another volume is linked into a specific session or folder in the custom collection.



Content Categories

Native content: Sessions, folders, and files that were created or uploaded directly in the custom collection. These belong to the collection and are not linked from anywhere else.
Linked content: Sessions, folders, and files that originate in a source volume and are linked into the custom collection. They are displayed in the collection but owned by the source volume.
Added content: Files uploaded directly into a linked session or folder within the custom collection. They live in the collection only — they do not appear in the source volume. They behave like native files for editing purposes.



Records (Metadata)

Source records: Records, like participant metadata, that belong to the source volume and move with the linked content. They appear in the collection as read-only and are not edittable.
Supplementary records: Records created in the custom collection and manually assigned to linked content. They exist only within the collection and can be edited or removed by collaborators with write access to the collection.

title: Technology and Security
text:
Application
Datasets are organized into separate volumes with system-wide unique (integer) identifiers. Groups of data files related to a specific person or people (or non-human animal), date, time, and location are grouped into sessions (slots) within a volume. Individual files (assets) of varying types are organized within a session (slot). Sessions (slots) and files (assets) are assigned system-wide unique (integer) identifiers.
Individual users and institutions are assigned system-wide unique identifiers and have some overlapping data elements (e.g., prename, sortname). Access privileges are granted hierarchically in a parent/child organization.

title: Technology and Security
text:
API
All Databrary frontend calls use the API. The volume/slot/asset identifier scheme described previously supports API calls of the following form:
https://nyu.databrary.org/volume/1/slot/9807?asset=9200
This call accesses the Databrary “leaf” logo in volume 1, slot (session) 9807, with asset ID 9200. Similarly, https://nyu.databrary.org/party/12 returns information about all of the Authorized Investigators who are authorized through party 12, The Pennsylvania State University.
Most, but not all of the Databrary API is documented. If it is necessary to change the API calls in the rewrite, then the API should be versioned, and the new system should support current API calls.

title: Technology and Security
text:
Backend Services
All audio and video files uploaded automatically generate transcoding jobs that are handled by the NYU HPC.
The system mints a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) when a volume is shared.
The system generates and updates standard bibliographic citations for a volume based on volume data and metadata.

title: Technology and Security
text:
System Roles

Super User
The system supports a small number of Super User accounts. Only an existing Super User can grant Super User privileges to another account holder. A Super User has the following privileges:

Editing user (party) account information
Changing a user’s parent (sponsor) and child (affiliate) links
Granting or removing system-wide access privileges
Monitoring and managing the health of the system as a whole, including restarting stalled video transcoding jobs via an admin dashboard
Generating email related to the process for requesting authorization from an institution for specific users



User
The system supports user accounts with the following features and privileges:

Account creation
Requesting authorization from an institution or individual (party)
Editing user profile information (ORCID, web site, social media, additional email accounts, department)
Two tiers of access: Authorized Investigators and Supervised Researchers

Authorized Investigators are specifically linked to an authorizing institution (party) when the Super User establishes that link. Authorized Investigators can:

Create, edit, share, and unshare volumes
Create, edit, and delete sessions (slots) in volumes they own or co-own
Upload, download, modify, and delete files (assets) in sessions in volumes they own or co-own
Modify which other users (Authorized Investigators or Affiliates) have access to a volume, session (slot), or file (asset); this includes removing access.
With regard to Affiliate, Authorized Investigators determine:

The Affiliate’s level of access to all of Databrary (no access or full access to shared data)
The Affiliate’s level of access to the Authorized Investigator’s data (no access; read-only access; read/write access; manager access)

Modify the level (sharing release level) assigned to a session (slot) or file (asset)

Supervised Researchers’ privileges to access restricted data on Databrary are specifically linked to one or more Authorized Investigators. The Authorized Investigator controls that link. Links should expire on a regular (timed) basis. When linked to an Authorized Investigator, Affiliates have the level of access granted by that Authorized Investigator to:

Databrary as a whole (default is none)
to specific volumes owned by the Authorized Investigator.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
I. Data Security and Technical Requirements
Copying and/or downloading content from Databrary must be accomplished in a manner that safeguards the content, and the research participants involved. Institutions and their Authorized Investigators and Affiliates agree to strictly abide by the following requirements, and to allow NYU, from time to time, to reasonably audit compliance.
For purposes of these requirements, “Databrary Content” means any potentially identifiable data obtained from Databrary, including, but not limited to, audiovisual recordings, frame captures, still images, audio tracks, transcripts, annotations, behavioral codings, metadata, or any derivatives created from or linked to those materials. “Databrary Content” also includes any study data (for example, surveys, assessments, ratings, or notes) that can be associated, directly or indirectly, with an identifiable participant appearing in the Databrary materials. “Databrary Content” does not include data for which participants have provided explicit, documented consent for unrestricted public use for teaching and learning purposes.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
1. Encryption

Encryption at Rest: All copies of Databrary Content (including backups) must be stored on systems under the Institution’s control that use strong encryption (e.g., full-disk encryption like BitLocker or FileVault, or encrypted containers).
Encryption in Transit: Databrary Content must only be transmitted using secure, encrypted channels (e.g., Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP), dedicated secure transfer services, or a secure Virtual Private Network (VPN)).



2. Access Control

Principle of Least Privilege: Access to Databrary Content (including viewing, copying, exporting, downloading, or otherwise processing, collectively, “Processing”) must be restricted solely to those Authorized Investigators and Affiliates sponsored by the Institution.
Strong Authentication: Access must be protected by strong, unique passwords (meeting industry best practices for specific complexity requirements) and multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Access Logging and Auditability: All access to and Processing of Databrary Content must be logged in a manner that records, at minimum, the user account, timestamp, file(s) accessed, and action(s) taken. The Institution agrees to retain these logs in accordance with its records retention schedule and to make such logs available to NYU upon reasonable request for audit or incident response purposes. These logs may not be altered or deleted except in accordance with that retention schedule.



3. Approved Storage Locations

Databrary Content must be stored solely on servers or secure cloud environments that are managed by the Institution, and expressly approved by the Institution’s IT/Security Office as appropriate for storage of sensitive data.
Prohibition on Unauthorized Devices: Databrary Content, including any copies or extracts, may only be stored in locations (including on-premises systems or Institution-managed cloud environments) that are owned, managed, and administered by the Institution. Databrary Content may not be stored on personally owned or personally managed devices or in any consumer or personal cloud service.
Physical Security: Any physical location where Databrary Content is stored or can be accessed must have access controls that restrict entry to authorized personnel only (e.g., keycard or biometric access controls, visitor logs).



4. Security Software

All devices used to access or store Databrary Content must have up-to-date operating systems and security software (e.g., antivirus/anti-malware protection) that are managed and configured by the Institution and prescribed by the Institution’s IT/security office.
Monitoring and Alerting: The Institution must maintain reasonable technical safeguards to detect and alert on suspicious activity involving Databrary Content, including but not limited to, unauthorized access attempts, atypical download behavior, or attempts to disable or otherwise circumvent security controls.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
1. De-identification/Coding

If any contact identifiers (full names, addresses) are provided alongside the Databrary Content containing identifiable individuals, they must be stored separately from the main working copies of Databrary Content.
A secure “key” file linking Databrary Content to identifiers must be stored separately from the Databrary Content itself, in a restricted and encrypted location that meets the same technical and access control requirements set out in this document.
To the degree possible, analyses must only be conducted on the minimum number of identifiers (birthdate, name, faces, voices) needed, for the minimum duration of time needed.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
2. Prohibition of Identification

Authorized Investigators and Affiliates are explicitly prohibited from attempting to re-identify individuals in the Databrary Contentor linking theDatabrary Content with other publicly available information to establish identity.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
3. Prohibition of Unauthorized Sharing/Disclosure

Authorized Investigators and Affiliates agree not to share, copy, or distribute the Databrary Content or any portion thereof to anyone outside the approved list of research personnel, including for presentations, teaching, or non-research purposes, except where such sharing is expressly authorized in the informed consent of the participant(s) whose data are included.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
4. Data Retention and Destruction:

Institutions and Authorized Investigators and Affiliates agree that all Databrary Content in their possession will have a defined destruction date of (a) the conclusion of the approved research project or (b) five years from the date of access. Extensions may be requested of the Databrary team at their full discretion, only for appropriate research reasons
Upon or before that destruction date, Institutions and Authorized Investigators and Affiliates agree to securely destroy or purge all copies of the Databrary Content from all storage media, including backups, in a manner consistent with the Institution’s data sanitization standards and, where feasible, NIST SP 800-88 Secure Media Sanitization Guidelines. Institutions and Authorized Investigators and Affiliates also agree to provide, upon NYU’s request, written certification from the Institution confirming that such destruction has been completed.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
1. Data Breach Reporting

In the event of a Security Incident or Data Breach, you must immediately notify the Institution’s designated IT contact, ideally within 24 hours of discovering the event. The Institution’s IT representative must then provide immediate notice to NYU of the breach or suspected breach.
The Breach Reporting must include, at minimum, a summary of the Incident, the date and time of discovery, the systems involved, the categories of Databrary Content exposed or suspected to be exposed, and any relevant access logs or audit trails associated with the Incident.

title: Data Security and Technical Requirements
text:
2. Compliance with Regulations

You and your Institution warrant that you will adhere to strict compliance with all applicable federal, state, and institutional regulations for human subjects research and data privacy (e.g., the Common Rule, institutional policies, and potentially GDPR or other applicable privacy laws depending on the location of the participants or researchers).

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Data Practices FAQs

Does Databrary offer “blind review”?
Databrary is a restricted access data repository that promotes the storage and sharing of identifiable and sensitive data. As such, Databrary has unique policies to protect the privacy of research participants. These policies govern who can access identifiable data and under what circumstances. The policies are codified in a formal access agreement that binds NYU, Databrary’s parent institution, and similar institutions where Databrary’s users conduct research. For the forseeable future, these policies make it impossible to support full double-blinded anonymous review of data and materials.
While some data and materials are shared with the public, Databrary restricts access to sensitive and identifiable information to people who have received authorization from an institution or to those whose access is supervised by an authorized investigator. Only authorized investigators can create and share datasets. Dataset creators, not Databrary, determine what level of sharing is appropriate for individual data files and for datasets as a whole.
So, the level of access a reviewer can have to a dataset depends on two things: Has the dataset been shared with the Databrary community? Does the reviewer have authorization from an institution to view restricted data or materials?
If both answers are yes, the reviewer may fully vet a shared dataset. Databrary does not report on access to specific datasets, so the reviewer can remain anonymous. Databrary does not mask the identities of dataset owners, so the blinding is only one-way.
If the dataset is shared, but the reviewer does not have authorization from an institution, the reviewer can confirm that a shared dataset exists, that the dataset has a persistent identifier, and that the dataset has a specific number of shared restricted access files. The reviewer may also examine any items that are shared with the public, stimuli, protocol, aggregated and de-identified datasets, etc.


I have a dataset that has been completely collected. Now we are ready to share with Databrary. What do I do?
Send an email to Databrary so they may assist you and determine next steps. You will need to include answers to the following questions:

What is the name and email address for PI for this project?

Do you have permission to share these data with the Databrary community?

Was a Data Sharing Release form or something similar completed at the time of data collection?

Do you have permission from your IRB or Research Ethics Board used at your institution to share this data with Databrary?


How many files are there for this dataset?

What file types do you have (e.g. .mov, .mp4, .mp3, .pdf, .xls)?
What is the total size of dataset (X GB)?

How many different sessions/participants do you have?

Do you have study documentation materials to share (e.g. data collection instructions, survey questions) in addition to the videos collected for the study?



Is there a storage capacity limit for each project?
At the moment, no. When we implement our fee-for-service/subscription model later in 2026, we will likely impose project, researcher, and institution level storage limits for new projects that do not pay or subscribe.


Is there a maximum file size? We have some multigig videos and want to check ahead of time if there is a limit
At the moment, no. However, we can not guarantee that large videos will transcode or stream well.
If you need to download videos in bulk or large videos, please consider using the databraryr package. It can be much faster than the web application.

Grant-Related Support
Many users want to know how to incorporate data sharing using Databrary in funding proposals to agencies like the U.S. National Science Foundation or National Institutes of Health.
Researchers should confirm funding agency, directorate, or program-specific resource sharing plans or data management plan requirements.

Data Management Plan Template
Below is boilerplate language prepared by Databrary that researchers can use to help draft data management or resource sharing plans. This document is intended to help researchers who plan to store and share video data in Databrary prepare grant materials for submission. The material here is particularly suited to NSF application requirements, but similar language can be adapted for NIH grants as well as private foundations.
Please contact us at contact@databrary.org for further assistance.
Researchers should confirm their institution, agency, directorate, or program-specific resource sharing plan or data management plan requirements.
Here are some resources to NIH’s and NSF’s data management plans.


Data Formats
Databrary transcodes all deposited video data into standard and HTML5-compatible formats, currently H.264+AAC as MP4. It stores the original video file along with the transformed, web accessible video file. Databrary stores other data in their original formats (e.g., .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .txt, .csv, .pdf, .jpg, .png). As standards for preferred video file formats change over time, Databrary will perform file format migrations to those preferred formats.


Metadata
Databrary takes and stores metadata related to a full dataset (e.g., title, authors, related publication, description of study, keywords or tags, associated URLs), individual study sessions (e.g. metadata related to participants, study groups and conditions, location, language, and session date and tasks), and video files (e.g., title, duration, tags) related to a dataset.
Metadata is added through a user-friendly web interface where auto-completion, suggested terms, and integration with third party services (e.g., CrossRef) guide users through its creation. Metadata may be accessed through the web interface, via API, or downloaded as a comma separated values (CSV) file.


Documentation
Data owners can upload and store on Databrary any number of related documents that assist other researchers in understanding their data (e.g. study protocol, coding manuals, output from video coding software, and procedural videos).
These documents can be associated with the dataset as a whole, or with individual sessions within the dataset.


Policies for Access and Sharing
Data will be stored with, and shared through, Databrary. Researchers are asked to avoid the inclusion of extraneous personally identifiable information (PII) in videos uploaded to Databrary. However, given the nature of video, it might still be possible to identify individuals based on first names, facial features, or details of the environment. Because of this, sensitive or identifiable data shared with Databrary will only be viewable and downloadable to authorized users who have been granted secure access by Databrary’s administrators. Select data may be made available to the public, but only as determined by the researcher and on the basis of participant permission. Only researchers with Principal Investigator status from institutions with Institutional Review Boards or similar review entities, or researchers affiliated with Principal Investigators, will be authorized for access.
Authorized users will be required to sign a user agreement that specifies that they will:

Be responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of the data;
Abide by ethical principles for treatment of human subjects as mandated by their local Institutional Review Boards;
Agree not use the data for commercial purposes; and
Treat Databrary data with the same high standard of care that they treat data collected in their own laboratory.

Although Databrary will store complete study data, only videos and other identifiable data that have been permissioned for sharing by all the depicted individuals in each recording will be made available to the community of authorized users.
Databrary has developed template Sharing Release forms that contributors can add to their IRB protocol. These forms allow researchers to ask participants for permission to share their data.
Data owners can choose to share their data at any point, either as they collect their data, or only once data collection has completed.


Policies and Provisions for Reuse and Redistribution
Access to videos and metadata will be available for educational and research purposes, subject to participant consent. Such access will be provided using the Databrary web-based application. Materials generated under the project will be disseminated in accordance with the policies of the grant-giving organization and participating institutions.
Publication of data shall occur during the project, if appropriate, or at the end of the project, consistent with normal scientific practices.


Plans for Archiving and Preservation
Data in Databrary will be preserved indefinitely in a secure data storage facility at New York University. The facility is managed by the university’s Information Technology Services department.
Central IT staff handle storage, network, and backup systems. NYU does routine tape backups that are stored off site and performs regular file fixity checks to monitor the integrity of stored assets.


Versioning of Stored Assets
Files uploaded to Databrary are assigned a unique identifier and have metadata associating them to files that are uploaded to replace them. Though only the latest version of a file is exposed to Databrary site users.Once files are uploaded, they are never deleted.


Data Security
Data and metadata stored in Databrary are subject to the security policies and best practices implemented by NYU. For more information about these policies and services, please visit NYU ITS Computer & Network Security.
